work.now: What I work on at VB Group
work.caseTitle: The case: tickets in, invoices out
work.caseSub: Integration between a ticketing platform and an invoicing ERP.
work.caseText: Ticket sales and handling fees came out of an events platform; an invoicing ERP needed them as simplified invoices, with VAT split the way an accountant expects. I built the layer between them.
work.caseHold: Ticket sales used to be passed to accounting by hand to generate simplified invoices. I built the integration that takes ticket sales, handling fees, merchandise and refunds and maps them to the fields the invoicing API needs. I had to work with two unfamiliar APIs and learn enough accounting to understand the data. I made direct requests and compared the responses to see how each system represented the same sale. Rounding caused problems too: the sales API sent rounded amounts, and the invoicing API recalculated them. I had to find a way to get more decimal places from the source so the amounts would match. Working with both APIs taught me how to test an integration when I do not control either system.

about.title: Hi, I’m Brad.
about.lede: Full-stack developer in Madrid. I like the parts nobody sees until they break. I build and maintain software in production, and I care most about data models, integrations and the standards that keep a growing team’s code in shape.
about.security: I trained in offensive security, and it changed how I write and review code: I read my own endpoints the way an attacker would.
about.knowTitle: What I know, and how well
about.knowLede: Kept apart on purpose: what I run in production, what I chose for my own projects, and what I used before or taught.

cases.problemSub: Two requests, one slot, a few milliseconds apart.
cases.problemText: Both requests read that the slot is free, both insert, and the court is sold twice. Reading, checking and inserting is exactly the code that fails under load.
cases.problemHold: My mother told me she and a neighbour had tried to book the same court at the same time. The app gave them both an error, and neither got the booking. That got me wondering how to handle two people trying to book the same slot. I built Reservas to try it out and find a way for one booking to succeed without saving duplicates.
cases.fixSub: The race from the test suite, in your browser.
cases.decisionsSub: Each has a record in docs/adr, with what I rejected.
cases.d1t: PostgreSQL decides who gets the court
cases.d1w: Production uses an EXCLUDE constraint on court and time range. It keeps working even if someone adds another route that inserts bookings tomorrow. Pessimistic and optimistic versions exist too, and pass the same tests.
cases.d1r: checking only in the application, SERIALIZABLE for every transaction, an in-memory mutex that cannot see other Vercel instances.
cases.d2w: A random 32-byte token in an HttpOnly __Host- cookie, stored hashed. Logout and sign out everywhere revoke instantly. CSRF is covered by SameSite=Lax plus an Origin check.
cases.d2r: JWT in localStorage, readable by any XSS, and JWT in a cookie, which still cannot be revoked before it expires.
cases.d3t: One Zod contract, mappers at every border
cases.d3w: The same schemas validate requests on the server and responses on the client. Changing a field touches three places, and nothing compiles until they agree.
cases.d3r: hand-written types on each side that drift apart silently.
cases.resultSub: Three strategies, the same fifteen tests, a real database.
cases.learnedHold1: I used to stick to the same structure in every project. Researching other approaches and writing ADRs helped me choose an architecture based on what the project needs.
cases.learnedHold2: Reading the code, I found that the login rate limiter could be counting the proxy's IP address instead of the client's. Logging in manually could work fine while the limit was being applied incorrectly. I fixed it and added tests with different IP addresses and simultaneous requests. I also ran them against the old code to check that they failed there. I would do the same in a team: check that a new regression test catches the original bug, especially with concurrency or proxies.
cases.casinoWhat: What it does and what I learned
cases.casinoText: Blackjack, roulette and slots with play money. There is no backend of my own: Firestore security rules decide what each player can read and write, so no one can see or change another player’s data. The rules also keep a balance from going below zero, but the chips have no real value, and a player can still change their own.
cases.casinoHold: The casino was one of the ideas my school suggested. I chose it because it sounded fun to build while learning. I had used Firebase before, but Angular and TypeScript were new to me. Understanding standalone components and how they fit together took time. So did the roulette logic and the scratch-off animation. I worked it out bit by bit, putting in the hours. I was working while building it, so I could put what I learned in each place to use in the other. The experience of connecting the app to an external database was particularly useful. Later, I refreshed the design to see what I could improve with more experience.
